text: Most of my stories end with a closed sign. This one doesn't. This is the one that got away.
I'm Sam. This is Last Receipt. Tonight, how Lego almost went bankrupt, and the very simple question that saved it.
That's the whole idea. One system. Every piece works with every other piece. A brick from 1958 still fits a brick from this morning.
Here's the thing. Lego decided the brick was the problem. The brick was the only thing nobody else had.
Now watch this. This is the moment where most of my stories go wrong. The company panics, cuts the wrong thing, sells the best piece, and the countdown begins.
And then he asked the question that saved the company. What are we actually good at?
And the answer they all gave was embarrassingly simple. They wanted bricks.
That click is the same click it was in 1958. Lego didn't need a new sound. It needed to stop being embarrassed by the old one.
So what saved Lego? Not a new product. Not a genius invention. It was a company remembering what it already was.
Lego almost died chasing everything it wasn't. It came back by doing the one thing nobody else could do.
If you're in a business that's struggling, it's worth asking Lego's question. What are we actually good at? Then do more of that.
